content: Administer an intravenous bolus of pyridoxine over a period of 3 to 5 minutes. The dose of pyridoxine should be calculated on a gram-per-gram basis equivalent to the ingested isoniazid dose. If the amount of isoniazid ingested is unknown, an initial intravenous bolus of 5 grams of pyridoxine for adults or 80 mg/kg for children is recommended. If seizures persist, the pyridoxine dose may be repeated. It is uncommon to require more than 10 grams of pyridoxine. The maximum safe dose of pyridoxine in cases of isoniazid toxicity has not been established. If the patient does not respond to pyridoxine, diazepam may be administered. Phenytoin should be used with caution, as isoniazid interferes with phenytoin metabolism. Blood should be typed and cross-matched in preparation for potential hemodialysis. Patients with severe isoniazid intoxication are likely to experience hypoventilation. In such cases, the administration of sodium bicarbonate can exacerbate hypercarbia. Ventilation must be carefully monitored by measuring blood carbon dioxide levels and supported mechanically if respiratory insufficiency occurs. Both peritoneal and hemodialysis have been utilized in the management of isoniazid overdose. However, these procedures are generally unnecessary if seizures and acidosis are controlled with pyridoxine, diazepam, and bicarbonate. Isoniazid inhibits the synthesis of mycolic acids, which are essential components of the bacterial cell wall. At therapeutic levels, isoniazid is bactericidal against actively growing intracellular and extracellular Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Resistance to isoniazid develops rapidly when it is used as monotherapy. Isoniazid is the hydrazide of isonicotinic acid. It is chemically known as isonicotinyl hydrazine or isonicotinic acid hydrazide. It is odorless and appears as a colorless or white crystalline powder or white crystals. It is freely soluble in water, sparingly soluble in alcohol, and slightly soluble in chloroform and ether. Isoniazid is slowly affected by exposure to air and light. During manufacturing, the air in the container is replaced with nitrogen. The pH is adjusted to 6 to 7 using sodium hydroxide or hydrochloric acid. Two standardized in vitro susceptibility methods are available for testing isoniazid against Mycobacterium tuberculosis. The minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) values are determined by comparing the growth of organisms in drug-containing media to control cultures. Mycobacterial growth in the presence of the drug at levels ≥1% of the control indicates resistance. Strict adherence to the manufacturer’s instructions for sample processing and data interpretation is required for these assays. Susceptibility test results obtained by different methods cannot be compared unless equivalent drug concentrations are evaluated. Isoniazid acts against actively growing tubercle bacilli. After oral administration, peak blood levels are achieved within 1 to 2 hours and decline to 50% or less within 6 hours. The drug diffuses readily into all body fluids (including cerebrospinal, pleural, and ascitic fluids), tissues, organs, and excreta (such as saliva, sputum, and feces). It crosses the placental barrier and is present in milk at concentrations comparable to plasma levels. Between 50% and 70% of an isoniazid dose is excreted in the urine within 24 hours. Isoniazid is primarily metabolized by acetylation and dehydrazination. The rate of acetylation is genetically determined. Approximately 50% of Black and Caucasian individuals are slow acetylators, while the remainder are rapid acetylators. The majority of Eskimos and Orientals are rapid acetylators. The rate of acetylation does not significantly alter the effectiveness of isoniazid therapy when administered daily. However, slow acetylation may result in higher blood levels of the drug, increasing the risk of toxic reactions. Pyridoxine (vitamin B6) deficiency is sometimes observed in adults receiving high doses of isoniazid, likely due to competition with pyridoxal phosphate for the enzyme apotryptophanase. Isoniazid has been shown to induce pulmonary tumors in certain strains of mice. However, it has not been demonstrated to be carcinogenic in humans. A case of mesothelioma in a child with prenatal exposure to isoniazid and no other apparent risk factors has been reported. Isoniazid has been found to be weakly mutagenic in certain strains of Salmonella typhimurium (Ames assay) without metabolic activation. Isoniazid injection is available for intramuscular use in 10 mL vials, providing 100 mg of isoniazid per mL. It should be stored at 20° to 25°C (68° to 77°F) and protected from light. There is limited information regarding clinical studies, patient counseling, and alcohol interactions with isoniazid injection. The brand name for isoniazid is Nydrazid.
